abstract: Relating non-invasive observations of human brain plasticity to cellular processes identified in animal models remains a major challenge in neuroscience. We address this challenge by introducing a paradigm for studying motor skill acquisition across species. We designed a human chopstick grasping task modeled after the rodent single-pellet reaching task, resulting in a comparable sequence of reach-to-grasp movements across species. We studied 48 young adult male C57BL/6N mice and 71 young men, comparing trained groups with untrained controls. In both mice and humans, structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before, during, and after motor training. The functional form of behavioral performance gains on the trained task was highly similar across species. In trained compared to control mice, analysis of the early learning interval revealed decreases in regional volume in contralateral primary motor and forelimb somatosensory cortices, with greater volume reductions in primary motor cortex associated with better reaching performance. In humans, performance gains transferred to other chopstick tasks but not to general dexterity, and no reliable changes in gray matter volume were observed. Quantitative MRI, however, revealed early training-related changes in tissue-sensitive measures, including increases in magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) and longitudinal relaxation rate (R1) in contralateral motor and frontal regions, potentially reflecting an increase in intracortical myelin. Thus, early structural changes in the contralateral motor cortex were detected in both species, but the degree to which these changes reflect a common biological mechanism is unclear. We conclude that the present cross-species paradigm provides a viable starting point for studying brain plasticity across species. Future work needs to relate macroscopic structural changes more directly to cellular processes by applying longitudinal microscopic imaging and MRI in the same animals.
